record.paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
record.original_question: How can large, accessible family-based cohorts and methods that combine family-based and population-based data be built and analyzed so that complex-trait studies can exploit Mendelian transmission and parental genotypes to separate causal from confounding effects and direct from indirect genetic effects?

evidence.quote: Accessible resources with an abundance of related individuals, on the scale of contemporary large-scale biobanks [22, 23], with rich genotypic and phenotypic data, could be a major force advancing the field. Unfortunately, such resources are still scarce (open problem #6: family-based vs. population-based cohorts).
methods combining and extracting signal from both family- and population-based data could be highly beneficial to the field.
Common analytical methods such as GWAS do not distinguish between direct and indirect genetic effects, and it is still very much an open challenge to effectively dissect the two.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a complex (polygenic) quantitative or binary trait Y measured on individuals in a population, together with their genome-wide genotypes G. In a standard population-based genome-wide association study (GWAS), one estimates, for each variant j, an effect β_j by regressing Y on G_j (with covariates). This estimated effect conflates: (i) the direct genetic effect (the causal effect of the individual's own allele on their own phenotype), (ii) indirect genetic effects (effects of relatives' genotypes acting through the environment, e.g., parental nurture), (iii) effects of population structure, assortative mating, and other sources of gene–environment confounding.

By contrast, in a family-based design with genotyped parent–offspring trios, Mendelian transmission provides, conditional on parental genotypes, a randomized assignment of the transmitted allele to the offspring; regressing offspring phenotype on transmitted vs. non-transmitted parental alleles permits unbiased estimation of direct effects and, via the non-transmitted alleles, of indirect (e.g., parental) effects. Such trio/sibship cohorts are however much smaller than population biobanks.

Formulate and solve the following problem:

(a) Design a statistical estimation framework that takes as input a large population-based cohort of unrelated individuals together with a (substantially smaller) family-based cohort of related individuals (e.g., parent–offspring trios, sibling pairs, or extended pedigrees), each with genome-wide genotypes and trait measurements, and that produces, for every variant or for genome-wide polygenic predictors, separate consistent estimators of (1) the direct genetic effect, (2) the indirect (parental/sibling) genetic effect, and (3) bias terms due to population stratification and assortative mating.

(b) Establish identifiability conditions and derive the asymptotic efficiency of the combined estimator relative to (i) the family-only estimator and (ii) the population-only estimator, as a function of the relative sample sizes, the heritability, and the magnitude of indirect effects and confounding.

(c) Provide a concrete construction (with proofs of consistency) showing how Mendelian transmission within the family subset can be used to debias the larger population-based estimates, including a procedure for constructing polygenic scores whose predictive accuracy reflects only direct genetic effects.

Equivalently: give a method, together with a theoretical guarantee, for using parental genotypes and Mendelian segregation to separate causal direct genetic effects from confounding and indirect genetic effects in complex-trait studies that pool family-based and population-based data.
artifact.status_search_result: Methods for separating direct from indirect genetic effects using family-based designs (e.g., Young et al.'s SNIPar/FGWAS, Kong et al.'s non-transmitted alleles approach, and Howe et al.'s within-sibship GWAS) have made substantial progress, and growing family resources (deCODE, MoBa, UK Biobank sibling subsets) have been used to combine family- and population-based signals. However, no general, fully accepted framework yet provides scalable, unbiased separation of direct, indirect, and stratification effects at biobank scale, and the problem is still discussed as open in recent reviews (2023–2025).

status_evidence.title: Relatedness disequilibrium regression and family-based GWAS (Young et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: We present a method (SNIPar) that uses parental genotypes (observed or imputed) to estimate direct genetic effects, separating them from indirect effects and demography.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress on separating direct from indirect effects using family data.

status_evidence.title: Within-sibship GWAS (Howe et al., Nature Genetics 2022)
status_evidence.snippet: Within-sibship analyses across 178,000 siblings show that population-based GWAS estimates are biased by indirect effects and assortative mating for several traits.
status_evidence.claim: Confirms that conventional GWAS conflates direct and indirect effects; family-based correction reduces, but does not eliminate, the problem.

status_evidence.title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics – problem context
status_evidence.snippet: Accessible large family-based resources are still scarce; methods combining family- and population-based data could be highly beneficial; dissecting direct vs indirect effects remains an open challenge.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is described as open.
